chapter_text:
CHAPTER 15 - CIRCULATION OF BODY FLUIDS

Introduction

Every living cell of the human body must be constantly supplied with oxygen and nutrients and must have its wastes carried away. In a large multicellular animal, simple diffusion is far too slow to reach the deep tissues, so a transport system is needed. The CIRCULATORY SYSTEM is this internal transport network. It uses fluids - mainly BLOOD, and also LYMPH and tissue fluid - pumped by the HEART through a system of BLOOD VESSELS to reach every part of the body. This chapter describes body fluids and their circulation, the composition and functions of blood, blood groups and transfusion, blood clotting, the lymphatic system, the structure and working of the human heart, the cardiac cycle, double circulation, the conducting system that sets the heartbeat, the different blood vessels, blood pressure and its regulation, and some common disorders of the circulatory system.

15.1 BODY FLUIDS AND TYPES OF CIRCULATORY SYSTEMS

The body fluids of animals include BLOOD, TISSUE FLUID (also called interstitial fluid) and LYMPH. Blood flows within vessels; tissue fluid bathes the cells directly; and lymph is the fluid that drains from the tissue spaces back towards the blood. Together these fluids link every cell to the organs of exchange - the lungs, the intestine, the kidneys and the skin.

Animals show two broad kinds of circulation. In an OPEN CIRCULATORY SYSTEM, seen in insects, prawns and many other arthropods and molluscs, the heart pumps blood (called haemolymph) into open spaces called SINUSES or the body cavity (haemocoel). The blood bathes the tissues directly and returns to the heart. There are no true capillaries, blood flow is slow and pressure is low. In a CLOSED CIRCULATORY SYSTEM, seen in earthworms, all vertebrates and humans, the blood always flows inside a continuous network of vessels - arteries, veins and capillaries. It never comes into direct contact with the tissues; exchange takes place across the thin walls of the capillaries. A closed system allows faster flow, higher pressure and more precise control of blood distribution, which is essential for active animals.

15.2 COMPOSITION AND FUNCTIONS OF BLOOD

Blood is a fluid CONNECTIVE TISSUE. An adult human has about 5 to 6 litres of blood. It consists of a liquid matrix called PLASMA (about 55 per cent by volume) in which are suspended the FORMED ELEMENTS or blood cells (about 45 per cent).

PLASMA is a pale yellow fluid that is about 90 to 92 per cent water and 8 to 10 per cent dissolved substances. Its solutes include plasma PROTEINS (albumin, globulins and fibrinogen), inorganic salts (sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride, bicarbonate), nutrients (glucose, amino acids, fats), hormones, dissolved gases and nitrogenous wastes such as urea. Albumin maintains the osmotic pressure of blood; globulins include antibodies that fight infection; fibrinogen is needed for clotting. Plasma without the clotting proteins is called SERUM.

The FORMED ELEMENTS are of three kinds:

(a) RED BLOOD CELLS (RBCs) or ERYTHROCYTES. These are the most numerous cells - about 5 million per cubic millimetre of blood. In mammals a mature RBC is a biconcave disc WITHOUT a nucleus, which increases its surface area and flexibility. RBCs are red because they contain the pigment HAEMOGLOBIN, an iron-containing protein that binds and transports oxygen (as oxyhaemoglobin) and helps carry carbon dioxide. RBCs are made in the RED BONE MARROW and live about 120 days; old cells are destroyed in the spleen and liver. The spleen is often called the graveyard of RBCs.

(b) WHITE BLOOD CELLS (WBCs) or LEUCOCYTES. These are fewer - about 5000 to 9000 per cubic millimetre - and are nucleated and colourless. They defend the body against disease. WBCs are of two groups. GRANULOCYTES (with granular cytoplasm) are of three types: NEUTROPHILS, which are the most abundant and engulf bacteria by phagocytosis; EOSINOPHILS, which act in allergic reactions and against parasites; and BASOPHILS, which release histamine and heparin in inflammation. AGRANULOCYTES (without prominent granules) are of two types: LYMPHOCYTES, which produce antibodies and provide immunity; and MONOCYTES, the largest WBCs, which become macrophages and engulf germs and dead cells.

(c) PLATELETS or THROMBOCYTES. These are not whole cells but small fragments of larger bone-marrow cells (megakaryocytes). They number about 2.5 to 4 lakh per cubic millimetre and play a central role in BLOOD CLOTTING by plugging cuts and releasing clotting factors.

The FUNCTIONS OF BLOOD are many: it transports oxygen and carbon dioxide; carries digested nutrients from the intestine to the cells; carries wastes to the kidneys; distributes hormones; distributes heat and regulates body temperature; maintains water balance and pH; defends against disease through WBCs and antibodies; and prevents its own loss through clotting.

15.3 BLOOD GROUPS AND BLOOD TRANSFUSION

Human blood is classified into groups on the basis of ANTIGENS (special proteins) present on the surface of the red blood cells. The most important is the ABO SYSTEM discovered by Karl Landsteiner. There are two antigens, A and B, and two corresponding antibodies, anti-A (a) and anti-B (b), in the plasma.

- Group A: antigen A on RBC, antibody b in plasma.
- Group B: antigen B on RBC, antibody a in plasma.
- Group AB: both antigens A and B, no antibodies. AB is the UNIVERSAL RECIPIENT because it has no antibodies to attack donor cells.
- Group O: no antigens, both antibodies a and b. O is the UNIVERSAL DONOR because its cells carry no antigen to be attacked.

In a TRANSFUSION the donor's antigen must not meet the recipient's matching antibody, or the red cells clump together (AGGLUTINATION) and block vessels, which can be fatal. So blood groups must be carefully matched before transfusion.

The Rh FACTOR is another antigen, first found in the rhesus monkey. People who have it are Rh POSITIVE (Rh+); those who lack it are Rh NEGATIVE (Rh-). An Rh- person does not normally have anti-Rh antibodies but makes them if given Rh+ blood. This matters in pregnancy: if an Rh- mother carries an Rh+ foetus, her body may make anti-Rh antibodies that can harm a later Rh+ baby, a condition called ERYTHROBLASTOSIS FOETALIS.

15.4 BLOOD CLOTTING (COAGULATION)

When a blood vessel is cut, blood loss is stopped by CLOTTING. At the injury, platelets stick to the damaged surface and break down, releasing an enzyme (thromboplastin). With the help of calcium ions and other clotting factors, thromboplastin converts the inactive plasma protein PROTHROMBIN into the active enzyme THROMBIN. Thrombin then converts the soluble plasma protein FIBRINOGEN into insoluble threads of FIBRIN. These fibrin threads form a mesh that traps blood cells, forming the CLOT that seals the wound. In brief: platelets release thromboplastin; prothrombin becomes thrombin; fibrinogen becomes fibrin; the fibrin net makes the clot. Vitamin K and calcium are needed for normal clotting.

15.5 LYMPH AND THE LYMPHATIC SYSTEM

As blood flows through the capillaries, some plasma (without the large proteins and cells) leaks out into the tissue spaces to form TISSUE FLUID, which supplies the cells with nutrients and oxygen. Most of this fluid returns to the blood, but the rest is collected by fine, blind-ending LYMPH CAPILLARIES and is then called LYMPH. Lymph is a colourless fluid, similar to plasma but with fewer proteins, and it contains many lymphocytes.

The LYMPHATIC SYSTEM consists of lymph capillaries, larger lymph vessels, LYMPH NODES and organs such as the spleen, thymus and tonsils. Lymph flows only towards the heart and is finally emptied into the large veins near the neck. Its functions are to return tissue fluid and leaked proteins to the blood, to absorb digested fats from the intestine (through special lymph vessels called lacteals), and to defend the body - lymph nodes filter the lymph and add lymphocytes and antibodies to fight infection.

15.6 STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN HEART

The HEART is a hollow, muscular organ about the size of a clenched fist, lying in the chest between the two lungs, tilted slightly to the left. It is made of a special muscle called CARDIAC MUSCLE. The heart is enclosed in a double-walled membranous sac, the PERICARDIUM, which contains pericardial fluid that reduces friction as the heart beats.

The human heart has FOUR CHAMBERS: two upper thin-walled AURICLES (atria) and two lower thick-walled VENTRICLES. The left and right sides are completely separated by a partition (septum), so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood never mix.

VALVES keep the blood flowing in one direction only. Between the right auricle and right ventricle is the TRICUSPID VALVE (three flaps). Between the left auricle and left ventricle is the BICUSPID or MITRAL VALVE (two flaps). These are the atrioventricular valves. At the openings of the two great arteries leaving the ventricles are the SEMILUNAR VALVES - the pulmonary semilunar valve (at the pulmonary artery) and the aortic semilunar valve (at the aorta) - which prevent blood from flowing back into the ventricles. The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it must pump blood to the whole body.

Blood enters the heart as follows: the right auricle receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the superior and inferior VENAE CAVAE; the left auricle receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the PULMONARY VEINS. The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs through the PULMONARY ARTERY; the left ventricle pumps blood to the whole body through the AORTA.

15.7 THE CARDIAC CYCLE AND HEART SOUNDS

The sequence of events in one complete heartbeat is the CARDIAC CYCLE. It has two main phases: SYSTOLE (contraction, which pumps blood out) and DIASTOLE (relaxation, which lets blood fill in). In an adult at rest the heart beats about 72 times per minute, so one cardiac cycle takes about 0.8 second.

The cycle runs as follows. First both auricles contract (atrial systole) and push blood into the ventricles through the open atrioventricular valves. Then the ventricles contract (ventricular systole); the tricuspid and bicuspid valves snap shut, the semilunar valves open, and blood is forced into the pulmonary artery and the aorta. Finally the whole heart relaxes (diastole); the semilunar valves close, the atrioventricular valves open, and the chambers refill with blood. The cycle then repeats.

The closing of the valves produces the HEART SOUNDS heard through a stethoscope as "LUBB-DUPP". The first sound, LUBB, is low and long and is caused by the closure of the atrioventricular (tricuspid and bicuspid) valves at the start of ventricular systole. The second sound, DUPP, is short and sharp and is caused by the closure of the semilunar valves at the end of ventricular systole. The volume of blood pumped out by one ventricle in one beat is the STROKE VOLUME, and the amount pumped per minute is the CARDIAC OUTPUT (stroke volume multiplied by heart rate), about 5 litres per minute at rest.

15.8 DOUBLE CIRCULATION

In humans and other mammals the blood passes through the heart TWICE in one complete round of the body - this is DOUBLE CIRCULATION. It has two loops.

The PULMONARY CIRCULATION carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle through the pulmonary artery to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide, and returns the oxygenated blood through the pulmonary veins to the left auricle. The SYSTEMIC CIRCULATION carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle through the aorta to all the tissues of the body, and returns deoxygenated blood through the venae cavae to the right auricle.

Because the two sides of the heart are completely separated, oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are kept apart. This makes oxygen delivery efficient and supports the high energy needs of warm-blooded animals.

15.9 THE CONDUCTING SYSTEM AND REGULATION OF THE HEARTBEAT

The heart beats on its own, without any signal from the brain - it is MYOGENIC, meaning the beat originates in the heart muscle itself. This is controlled by a special CONDUCTING SYSTEM of modified cardiac muscle.

The beat begins in the SINO-ATRIAL (SA) NODE, a patch of tissue in the wall of the right auricle. Because it sets the rhythm, the SA node is called the PACEMAKER. The impulse it generates spreads over both auricles, making them contract, and reaches the ATRIO-VENTRICULAR (AV) NODE at the junction of the auricles and ventricles. From the AV node the impulse passes down the BUNDLE OF HIS in the septum, which divides into right and left branches, and finally spreads through the fine PURKINJE FIBRES into the walls of the ventricles, making them contract from the base upwards. In this way the auricles and ventricles contract in the correct order.

Although the heartbeat is myogenic, its rate is adjusted by nerves and hormones. The AUTONOMIC nervous system speeds up the heart (through sympathetic nerves) during exercise, fear or excitement, and slows it (through the parasympathetic vagus nerve) during rest. The hormone ADRENALINE also increases the heart rate.

The electrical activity of the heart can be recorded from the body surface as an ELECTROCARDIOGRAM (ECG or EKG). A normal ECG shows a series of waves: the P wave (contraction of the auricles), the QRS complex (contraction of the ventricles) and the T wave (relaxation of the ventricles). Doctors study the shape and timing of these waves to detect abnormal rhythms and other heart problems.

15.10 BLOOD VESSELS

Blood flows through three kinds of vessels. ARTERIES carry blood AWAY from the heart. They have thick, elastic, muscular walls and a narrow lumen to withstand the high pressure of blood pumped by the ventricles. Except for the pulmonary artery, arteries carry oxygenated blood. VEINS carry blood back TOWARDS the heart. They have thinner walls, a wider lumen, and VALVES that prevent the backflow of blood. Except for the pulmonary veins, veins carry deoxygenated blood. CAPILLARIES are the finest vessels, with walls only ONE cell thick. They connect the smallest arteries (arterioles) to the smallest veins (venules) and form networks in the tissues. It is across the thin capillary walls that oxygen, nutrients and wastes are actually exchanged between blood and cells.

15.11 BLOOD PRESSURE AND ITS REGULATION

BLOOD PRESSURE is the force exerted by the blood against the walls of the arteries. It is measured with an instrument called a SPHYGMOMANOMETER and expressed as two numbers. The higher figure is the SYSTOLIC pressure (when the ventricles contract) and the lower figure is the DIASTOLIC pressure (when the ventricles relax). A normal healthy adult has a blood pressure of about 120/80 mm of mercury (mm Hg).

Blood pressure is regulated so that the tissues always get enough blood. Pressure sensors (baroreceptors) in the walls of large arteries such as the aorta and the carotid detect changes and send signals to a control centre in the brain (the medulla). The centre then adjusts the heart rate, the force of the heartbeat and the width of the blood vessels (vasoconstriction or vasodilation). Hormones such as adrenaline and those from the kidneys also help control blood pressure by adjusting salt and water balance.

15.12 DISORDERS OF THE CIRCULATORY SYSTEM

HYPERTENSION (high blood pressure) is a persistent rise of blood pressure above the normal level (for example above 140/90 mm Hg). It usually has no obvious symptoms but strains the heart and vessels and can lead to heart and kidney disease and stroke.

ATHEROSCLEROSIS is the narrowing and hardening of arteries by the deposition of fatty material (cholesterol) and calcium in their walls. The narrowed, stiff arteries raise blood pressure and reduce blood flow.

A HEART ATTACK (myocardial infarction) happens when a coronary artery supplying the heart muscle is blocked, often by a clot on an atherosclerotic patch. The heart muscle beyond the block is starved of oxygen and part of it dies. A related condition, ANGINA, is chest pain caused when the heart muscle does not get enough blood. Sensible diet, regular exercise, avoiding tobacco and controlling body weight help keep the circulatory system healthy.

SUMMARY

- Body fluids (blood, tissue fluid, lymph) transport materials in the body. Circulation is OPEN (insects; blood in sinuses) or CLOSED (vertebrates and humans; blood in vessels).
- Blood is a fluid connective tissue: about 55 per cent PLASMA (water, proteins - albumin, globulin, fibrinogen - salts, nutrients, wastes) and 45 per cent FORMED ELEMENTS.
- RBCs (erythrocytes) are biconcave, non-nucleated, carry oxygen using haemoglobin, and live about 120 days. WBCs (leucocytes: neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, lymphocytes, monocytes) defend the body. Platelets help clotting.
- ABO blood groups (A, B, AB, O) depend on antigens on RBCs; O is the universal donor and AB the universal recipient. The Rh factor makes blood Rh+ or Rh-. Groups must be matched for transfusion.
- Clotting: platelets release thromboplastin; prothrombin becomes thrombin; fibrinogen becomes fibrin; the fibrin mesh forms the clot.
- Lymph is tissue fluid that drains into lymph vessels; the lymphatic system returns fluid and proteins to blood, absorbs fats, and provides defence.
- The heart has four chambers (two auricles, two ventricles), the tricuspid, bicuspid and semilunar valves, and is enclosed in the pericardium.
- The cardiac cycle has systole (contraction) and diastole (relaxation); valve closure gives the LUBB (AV valves) and DUPP (semilunar valves) heart sounds.
- Double circulation has a pulmonary loop (heart-lungs-heart) and a systemic loop (heart-body-heart), keeping oxygenated and deoxygenated blood apart.
- The heartbeat is myogenic: SA node (pacemaker) - AV node - bundle of His - Purkinje fibres; the ECG (P, QRS, T waves) records the heart's electrical activity.
- Arteries (thick, away from heart), veins (thinner, with valves, towards heart) and capillaries (one cell thick, site of exchange) form the vessels. Blood pressure (about 120/80 mm Hg) is measured with a sphygmomanometer and regulated by baroreceptors and the brain.
- Disorders include hypertension, atherosclerosis, angina and heart attack (myocardial infarction).

topics.name: Circulatory Systems and Composition of Blood
topics.description: Body fluids (blood, tissue fluid, lymph) and their circulation; open versus closed circulatory systems; blood as a fluid connective tissue; composition of blood - plasma and formed elements (RBCs/erythrocytes, WBCs/leucocytes and their types, platelets) and the functions of blood.

topics.name: Blood Groups, Clotting and Lymph
topics.description: ABO blood groups (antigens A/B and antibodies), the universal donor and recipient, the Rh factor and transfusion; the mechanism of blood clotting (platelets, prothrombin, thrombin, fibrinogen, fibrin); lymph and the lymphatic system and their functions.

topics.name: Structure of the Human Heart
topics.description: Structure of the human heart: four chambers (two auricles, two ventricles), the pericardium, and the valves - tricuspid, bicuspid (mitral) and semilunar - together with the great vessels entering and leaving the heart.

topics.name: The Cardiac Cycle and Double Circulation
topics.description: The cardiac cycle - systole and diastole, atrial and ventricular contraction, heart sounds (LUBB and DUPP), stroke volume and cardiac output; and double circulation through the pulmonary and systemic loops.

topics.name: The Conducting System and Heartbeat Regulation
topics.description: The myogenic heartbeat and the conducting system - SA node (pacemaker), AV node, bundle of His and Purkinje fibres; nervous and hormonal regulation of heart rate; and the electrocardiogram (ECG) with its P, QRS and T waves.

topics.name: Blood Vessels, Blood Pressure and Disorders
topics.description: Blood vessels - arteries, veins and capillaries and their structure; blood pressure (systolic and diastolic, 120/80 mm Hg) measured by a sphygmomanometer and its regulation; and disorders such as hypertension, atherosclerosis, angina and heart attack.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Circulation of Body Fluids (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Answer briefly and to the point for short-answer questions and in detail for long-answer questions. Draw and label diagrams where asked.

questions.question: Distinguish between an open and a closed circulatory system, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: In an OPEN circulatory system the heart pumps blood into open spaces or sinuses (haemocoel) where it bathes the tissues directly before returning to the heart; there are no true capillaries, and blood flow is slow with low pressure. Example: insects and prawns. In a CLOSED circulatory system the blood always flows within a continuous network of vessels - arteries, veins and capillaries - and exchange takes place across the thin capillary walls; flow is faster, pressure higher and distribution better controlled. Example: earthworm and all vertebrates including humans.
questions.explanation: Contrast vessels vs sinuses, flow, pressure and examples.

questions.question: Name the three types of formed elements in blood and state one function of each.
questions.answer: The three formed elements are: (1) Red blood cells (RBCs / erythrocytes) - transport oxygen using the pigment haemoglobin; (2) White blood cells (WBCs / leucocytes) - defend the body against disease by phagocytosis and by producing antibodies; (3) Platelets (thrombocytes) - help in blood clotting by plugging cuts and releasing clotting factors.
questions.explanation: RBC transport, WBC defence, platelet clotting.

questions.question: Why is blood group O called the universal donor and blood group AB the universal recipient?
questions.answer: Group O red cells carry NO A or B antigen on their surface, so when O blood is given to any recipient there is no antigen for the recipient's antibodies to attack; hence O is the universal donor. Group AB plasma contains NO anti-A or anti-B antibodies, so it will not attack the red cells of any donor group; hence AB is the universal recipient. (These simple rules ignore the Rh factor and are used only as a first guide.)
questions.explanation: O has no antigens; AB has no antibodies.

questions.question: Describe the mechanism of blood clotting, naming the substances involved.
questions.answer: When a blood vessel is cut, clotting seals the wound in a series of steps. (1) Platelets accumulate at the injury, stick to the damaged surface and break down, releasing an enzyme called THROMBOPLASTIN. (2) Thromboplastin, in the presence of CALCIUM IONS and other clotting factors, converts the inactive plasma protein PROTHROMBIN into the active enzyme THROMBIN. (3) Thrombin then converts the soluble plasma protein FIBRINOGEN into insoluble threads of FIBRIN. (4) The fibrin threads form a mesh that traps blood cells, producing the CLOT that plugs the wound and stops bleeding. Vitamin K and calcium are essential for normal clotting. In short: platelets -> thromboplastin; prothrombin -> thrombin; fibrinogen -> fibrin -> clot.
questions.explanation: Sequence: thromboplastin, prothrombin->thrombin, fibrinogen->fibrin->clot.

questions.question: Name the valves of the human heart and state the function of valves.
questions.answer: The heart has the TRICUSPID valve (between the right auricle and right ventricle), the BICUSPID or MITRAL valve (between the left auricle and left ventricle), and the SEMILUNAR valves at the openings of the pulmonary artery and the aorta. The function of the valves is to allow blood to flow in one direction only and to prevent the backflow of blood, so that blood moves forward through the heart and into the arteries.
questions.explanation: Tricuspid, bicuspid, semilunar; prevent backflow.

questions.question: Explain the cardiac cycle and describe how the two heart sounds are produced.
questions.answer: The cardiac cycle is the sequence of events in one complete heartbeat; it consists of SYSTOLE (contraction) and DIASTOLE (relaxation), and at 72 beats per minute one cycle takes about 0.8 second. First the two auricles contract (atrial systole) and push blood into the ventricles through the open atrioventricular valves. Next the ventricles contract (ventricular systole): the tricuspid and bicuspid valves snap shut, the semilunar valves open, and blood is forced into the pulmonary artery and the aorta. Finally the whole heart relaxes (diastole): the semilunar valves close, the atrioventricular valves open, and the chambers refill. The valve closures make the heart sounds. The first sound, LUBB, is low and long and is caused by the closure of the atrioventricular (tricuspid and bicuspid) valves at the start of ventricular systole. The second sound, DUPP, is short and sharp and is caused by the closure of the semilunar valves at the end of ventricular systole.
questions.explanation: Systole/diastole steps; LUBB = AV valves, DUPP = semilunar valves.

questions.question: What is double circulation? Name its two loops.
questions.answer: Double circulation means that in one complete round of the body the blood passes through the heart TWICE. It has two loops. The PULMONARY circulation carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs and returns oxygenated blood to the left auricle. The SYSTEMIC circulation carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to all body tissues and returns deoxygenated blood to the right auricle. Because the heart's two sides are separate, oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix.
questions.explanation: Blood through heart twice; pulmonary and systemic loops.

questions.question: Trace the path of an impulse through the conducting system of the heart.
questions.answer: The heartbeat is myogenic and its impulse follows a fixed path. It begins at the SINO-ATRIAL (SA) NODE in the wall of the right auricle, which is the pacemaker. The impulse spreads over both auricles (making them contract) and reaches the ATRIO-VENTRICULAR (AV) NODE. From the AV node it passes down the BUNDLE OF HIS in the septum, which divides into right and left branches, and finally spreads through the fine PURKINJE FIBRES into the ventricle walls, making the ventricles contract from the base upwards.
questions.explanation: SA node -> AV node -> bundle of His -> Purkinje fibres.

questions.question: Compare arteries and veins with respect to wall thickness, direction of flow and presence of valves.
questions.answer: ARTERIES carry blood AWAY from the heart; they have thick, elastic, muscular walls with a narrow lumen to withstand high pressure, and they have no valves along their length (except the semilunar valves at their origin). VEINS carry blood back TOWARDS the heart; they have thinner walls and a wider lumen and possess VALVES along their length to prevent the backflow of blood. Most arteries carry oxygenated blood (except the pulmonary artery) and most veins carry deoxygenated blood (except the pulmonary veins).
questions.explanation: Arteries thick, away, no valves; veins thinner, towards, with valves.

questions.question: What is blood pressure? Give the normal value and name the instrument used to measure it.
questions.answer: Blood pressure is the force exerted by the flowing blood against the walls of the arteries. It is expressed as two figures: the SYSTOLIC pressure (when the ventricles contract) over the DIASTOLIC pressure (when the ventricles relax). The normal value for a healthy adult is about 120/80 mm of mercury (mm Hg). It is measured with an instrument called a SPHYGMOMANOMETER. A persistent rise above normal is called hypertension.
questions.explanation: Force on artery walls; 120/80 mm Hg; sphygmomanometer.

questions.question: Why do large animals need a circulatory system?
questions.answer: In large multicellular animals the cells lie far from the surface, and simple diffusion is far too slow to supply oxygen and nutrients or to remove wastes from the deep tissues. A circulatory system provides an internal transport network that carries these materials quickly to and from every cell, keeping them alive and active.
questions.explanation: Diffusion is too slow for deep tissues.

questions.question: Name the three body fluids and state where each is found.
questions.answer: The three body fluids are: (1) BLOOD, which flows within the blood vessels; (2) TISSUE FLUID (interstitial fluid), which bathes the cells directly in the tissue spaces; and (3) LYMPH, which is the fluid collected from the tissue spaces into lymph vessels and returned towards the blood.
questions.explanation: Blood in vessels, tissue fluid around cells, lymph in lymph vessels.

questions.question: List any four functions of blood.
questions.answer: Four functions of blood are: (1) transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide; (2) transport of digested nutrients from the intestine to the cells and of wastes to the kidneys; (3) distribution of hormones and of heat to regulate body temperature; and (4) defence against disease through white blood cells and antibodies, together with clotting to prevent blood loss.
questions.explanation: Transport, temperature regulation, defence, clotting.

questions.question: Name the two groups of white blood cells and give the types in each.
questions.answer: White blood cells are grouped into GRANULOCYTES, which have granular cytoplasm and include neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils; and AGRANULOCYTES, which lack prominent granules and include lymphocytes and monocytes.
questions.explanation: Granulocytes: neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil. Agranulocytes: lymphocyte, monocyte.

questions.question: How is the structure of an RBC suited to its function?
questions.answer: A mammalian RBC is a biconcave disc without a nucleus. The biconcave shape gives it a large surface area for absorbing and releasing oxygen and makes it flexible enough to squeeze through narrow capillaries. The absence of a nucleus leaves more room for haemoglobin, the pigment that binds and carries oxygen. These features make the RBC an efficient oxygen carrier.
questions.explanation: Biconcave + no nucleus = more surface and more haemoglobin.

questions.question: What is the difference between plasma and serum?
questions.answer: Plasma is the whole liquid part of blood, containing water, proteins (including fibrinogen and other clotting factors), salts, nutrients and wastes. Serum is plasma from which the clotting proteins, chiefly fibrinogen, have been removed. In other words, serum is plasma without the clotting factors.
questions.explanation: Serum = plasma minus clotting proteins.

questions.question: Explain why blood groups must be matched before a transfusion.
questions.answer: Each blood group carries particular antigens on its red cells and particular antibodies in its plasma. If a donor's red cells carry an antigen that meets the recipient's matching antibody, the red cells clump together (agglutination) and can block blood vessels, which may be fatal. Therefore the donor and recipient blood groups (and the Rh factor) must be carefully matched before a transfusion so that no antigen meets its matching antibody.
questions.explanation: Mismatch causes agglutination; match antigen-antibody.

questions.question: What is erythroblastosis foetalis and how may it arise?
questions.answer: Erythroblastosis foetalis is a condition in which the red blood cells of an Rh-positive foetus are destroyed by antibodies from the mother. It can arise when an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive baby: some foetal Rh antigen may enter the mother's blood and cause her to make anti-Rh antibodies. In a later Rh-positive pregnancy these antibodies can cross into the foetus and destroy its red cells.
questions.explanation: Rh- mother makes anti-Rh antibodies that harm a later Rh+ baby.

questions.question: What is lymph and how is it formed?
questions.answer: Lymph is a colourless body fluid, similar to plasma but with fewer proteins and containing many lymphocytes. It is formed when some plasma (without the large proteins and cells) leaks out of the blood capillaries into the tissue spaces to form tissue fluid; the part of this fluid that is collected by the fine, blind-ending lymph capillaries is called lymph.
questions.explanation: Lymph = tissue fluid drained into lymph capillaries.

questions.question: State three functions of the lymphatic system.
questions.answer: Three functions of the lymphatic system are: (1) it returns tissue fluid and leaked proteins from the tissue spaces back to the blood; (2) it absorbs digested fats from the intestine through special lymph vessels called lacteals; and (3) it defends the body, as the lymph nodes filter the lymph and add lymphocytes and antibodies to fight infection.
questions.explanation: Return fluid/proteins, absorb fats, defence.

questions.question: Name the four chambers of the human heart.
questions.answer: The four chambers of the human heart are the two upper thin-walled AURICLES (the right auricle and the left auricle) and the two lower thick-walled VENTRICLES (the right ventricle and the left ventricle).
questions.explanation: Right and left auricles; right and left ventricles.

questions.question: Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than that of the right ventricle?
questions.answer: The left ventricle has to pump blood through the aorta to the whole body, which is a long path against considerable resistance, so it must generate a high pressure. The right ventricle only pumps blood a short distance to the nearby lungs at lower pressure. Because a stronger, more forceful contraction is needed on the left, the left ventricular wall is much thicker and more muscular.
questions.explanation: Left ventricle pumps to whole body at higher pressure.

questions.question: Trace the entry and exit of blood through the right side of the heart.
questions.answer: Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the RIGHT AURICLE through the superior and inferior venae cavae. From the right auricle it passes through the tricuspid valve into the RIGHT VENTRICLE. When the right ventricle contracts, the blood is pushed through the pulmonary semilunar valve into the PULMONARY ARTERY, which carries it to the lungs to be oxygenated.
questions.explanation: Venae cavae -> right auricle -> tricuspid -> right ventricle -> pulmonary artery.

questions.question: Distinguish between systole and diastole.
questions.answer: SYSTOLE is the phase of the cardiac cycle in which the heart muscle contracts and pumps blood out of the chambers - atrial systole empties the auricles into the ventricles and ventricular systole forces blood into the arteries. DIASTOLE is the phase in which the heart muscle relaxes, the chambers expand, and blood flows in to refill them. In short, systole is contraction (pumping) and diastole is relaxation (filling).
questions.explanation: Systole = contraction/pumping; diastole = relaxation/filling.

questions.question: What causes the two heart sounds LUBB and DUPP?
questions.answer: The heart sounds are caused by the closing of the valves. The first sound, LUBB, is low and long and is produced by the closure of the atrioventricular (tricuspid and bicuspid) valves at the beginning of ventricular systole. The second sound, DUPP, is short and sharp and is produced by the closure of the semilunar valves at the end of ventricular systole.
questions.explanation: LUBB = AV valves close; DUPP = semilunar valves close.

questions.question: Describe the two loops of double circulation.
questions.answer: Double circulation has two loops. In the PULMONARY circulation, deoxygenated blood is pumped from the right ventricle through the pulmonary artery to the lungs, where it is oxygenated, and returns through the pulmonary veins to the left auricle. In the SYSTEMIC circulation, oxygenated blood is pumped from the left ventricle through the aorta to all the body tissues, and deoxygenated blood returns through the venae cavae to the right auricle.
questions.explanation: Pulmonary: heart-lungs-heart; systemic: heart-body-heart.

questions.question: What is meant by a myogenic heartbeat?
questions.answer: A myogenic heartbeat is one that originates within the heart muscle itself rather than being started by a nerve impulse from the brain. In the human heart the beat begins at the sino-atrial (SA) node, a patch of special muscle in the right auricle, and then spreads through the conducting system. The heart therefore continues to beat rhythmically on its own, though nerves and hormones can adjust its rate.
questions.explanation: Beat originates in the heart muscle (SA node), not the brain.

questions.question: How is the heart rate regulated by nerves and hormones?
questions.answer: Although the beat is myogenic, its rate is adjusted by the autonomic nervous system and hormones. Sympathetic nerves speed up the heart during exercise, fear or excitement, while the parasympathetic vagus nerve slows it during rest. The hormone adrenaline, released in stress or activity, also raises the heart rate. Together these keep the heart's output matched to the body's needs.
questions.explanation: Sympathetic speeds up, vagus slows down, adrenaline speeds up.

questions.question: What is an ECG and what do its main waves represent?
questions.answer: An ECG (electrocardiogram) is a record of the electrical activity of the heart taken from the body surface. A normal ECG shows a series of waves: the P wave represents the contraction (depolarisation) of the auricles, the QRS complex represents the contraction of the ventricles, and the T wave represents the relaxation (repolarisation) of the ventricles. Doctors study the shape and timing of these waves to detect abnormal rhythms and other heart problems.
questions.explanation: P = auricles, QRS = ventricles contract, T = ventricles relax.

questions.question: Give three differences between arteries and capillaries.
questions.answer: Arteries are relatively large vessels with thick, elastic, muscular walls that carry blood away from the heart under high pressure; they do not exchange materials with the tissues. Capillaries are the finest vessels with walls only one cell thick; they connect arterioles to venules and it is across their thin walls that oxygen, nutrients and wastes are exchanged between blood and cells, under low pressure.
questions.explanation: Size, wall thickness, function (transport vs exchange).

questions.question: Explain what systolic and diastolic blood pressure mean.
questions.answer: Blood pressure is written as two figures, for example 120/80 mm Hg. The higher figure is the SYSTOLIC pressure, the pressure in the arteries when the ventricles contract and push blood out. The lower figure is the DIASTOLIC pressure, the pressure remaining in the arteries when the ventricles relax between beats. Together they describe the range of pressure in the arteries during one cardiac cycle.
questions.explanation: Systolic = ventricles contract; diastolic = ventricles relax.

questions.question: What is hypertension and why is it dangerous?
questions.answer: Hypertension is a persistent rise of blood pressure above the normal level, for example above 140/90 mm Hg. It usually gives no obvious symptoms, so it may go unnoticed, yet it constantly strains the heart and the blood vessels. Over time it can damage the arteries and lead to serious problems such as heart disease, kidney disease and stroke, which is why it is called a silent killer.
questions.explanation: Persistent high BP strains heart/vessels; leads to heart, kidney disease, stroke.

questions.question: Describe the composition of blood, naming the parts of plasma and the formed elements.
questions.answer: Blood is a fluid connective tissue of which an adult has about 5 to 6 litres. It has two main parts. PLASMA (about 55 per cent by volume) is a pale-yellow fluid, about 90 to 92 per cent water. Dissolved in it are plasma PROTEINS - albumin (maintains osmotic pressure), globulins (include antibodies) and fibrinogen (needed for clotting) - together with inorganic salts, nutrients (glucose, amino acids, fats), hormones, gases and wastes such as urea. The FORMED ELEMENTS (about 45 per cent) are of three kinds: RED BLOOD CELLS (erythrocytes), biconcave and non-nucleated, which carry oxygen using haemoglobin; WHITE BLOOD CELLS (leucocytes) - neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, lymphocytes and monocytes - which defend the body; and PLATELETS (thrombocytes), cell fragments that help in clotting.
questions.explanation: Plasma (water, proteins, salts, nutrients, wastes) + RBC, WBC, platelets.

questions.question: Describe the different types of white blood cells and the function of each.
questions.answer: White blood cells (leucocytes) are nucleated, colourless cells that defend the body. They fall into two groups. GRANULOCYTES have granular cytoplasm: NEUTROPHILS are the most abundant and engulf bacteria by phagocytosis; EOSINOPHILS act in allergic reactions and against parasites; BASOPHILS release histamine and heparin during inflammation. AGRANULOCYTES lack prominent granules: LYMPHOCYTES produce antibodies and provide immunity; MONOCYTES, the largest WBCs, become macrophages that engulf germs and dead cells. Together these cells protect the body against infection and disease.
questions.explanation: Neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil, lymphocyte, monocyte and their roles.

questions.question: Explain the ABO blood group system and the concept of universal donor and recipient.
questions.answer: In the ABO system, discovered by Landsteiner, blood is grouped by the antigens on the red cells and the antibodies in the plasma. Group A has antigen A and antibody anti-B; Group B has antigen B and antibody anti-A; Group AB has both antigens A and B and no antibodies; Group O has no antigen but both antibodies. Because group O red cells carry no A or B antigen, O blood can be given to any recipient without its cells being attacked - O is the UNIVERSAL DONOR. Because group AB plasma has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies, an AB person can receive blood of any group - AB is the UNIVERSAL RECIPIENT. In a transfusion the donor's antigen must not meet the recipient's matching antibody, or the cells agglutinate.
questions.explanation: A/B/AB/O antigens and antibodies; O donor, AB recipient.

questions.question: With reference to its chambers and valves, describe the structure of the human heart.
questions.answer: The human heart is a hollow muscular organ about the size of a fist, lying between the lungs and enclosed in a double-walled sac, the pericardium, which contains lubricating fluid. It has FOUR CHAMBERS: two upper thin-walled auricles and two lower thick-walled ventricles, with the left and right sides separated by a septum so that oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix. VALVES keep blood flowing one way: the TRICUSPID valve lies between the right auricle and right ventricle, the BICUSPID (mitral) valve between the left auricle and left ventricle, and the SEMILUNAR valves guard the openings of the pulmonary artery and the aorta. The right auricle receives deoxygenated blood from the venae cavae and the left auricle receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins; the right ventricle sends blood to the lungs and the left ventricle, with its thick wall, pumps blood to the whole body.
questions.explanation: Pericardium, four chambers, tricuspid/bicuspid/semilunar valves, vessels.

questions.question: Explain the cardiac cycle in sequence and relate it to the heart sounds.
questions.answer: The cardiac cycle is one complete heartbeat, made of systole (contraction) and diastole (relaxation); at 72 beats per minute it lasts about 0.8 second. First the auricles contract (atrial systole) and force blood into the ventricles through the open atrioventricular valves. Next the ventricles contract (ventricular systole): the tricuspid and bicuspid valves close (producing the first sound, LUBB) and the semilunar valves open, so blood is pushed into the pulmonary artery and the aorta. Then the whole heart relaxes (diastole): the semilunar valves close (producing the second sound, DUPP) and the atrioventricular valves open, allowing the chambers to refill. The cycle then repeats, and the alternating LUBB-DUPP is heard through a stethoscope.
questions.explanation: Atrial systole, ventricular systole (LUBB), diastole (DUPP).

questions.question: Describe the conducting system of the heart and how it coordinates the heartbeat.
questions.answer: The heartbeat is myogenic and is coordinated by a conducting system of modified cardiac muscle. Each beat begins at the SINO-ATRIAL (SA) NODE in the wall of the right auricle, the pacemaker that sets the rhythm. The impulse spreads over both auricles, making them contract, and reaches the ATRIO-VENTRICULAR (AV) NODE at the junction of the auricles and ventricles. From the AV node the impulse travels down the BUNDLE OF HIS in the septum, which splits into right and left branches, and finally spreads through the fine PURKINJE FIBRES into the ventricle walls, so the ventricles contract from the base upwards. This ordered pathway ensures that the auricles contract first and the ventricles afterwards, giving an efficient, coordinated beat. Nerves and the hormone adrenaline can adjust its rate.
questions.explanation: SA node -> AV node -> bundle of His -> Purkinje fibres; ordered contraction.

questions.question: Compare the structure and function of arteries, veins and capillaries.
questions.answer: Blood flows through three kinds of vessels. ARTERIES carry blood away from the heart; they have thick, elastic, muscular walls and a narrow lumen to withstand the high pressure of blood from the ventricles, and (except the pulmonary artery) carry oxygenated blood. VEINS carry blood back towards the heart; they have thinner walls, a wider lumen and valves that prevent backflow, and (except the pulmonary veins) carry deoxygenated blood. CAPILLARIES are the finest vessels, with walls just one cell thick; they link the arterioles to the venules and form networks in the tissues, and it is across their thin walls that oxygen, nutrients and wastes are actually exchanged between the blood and the cells. Thus arteries and veins transport blood, while capillaries carry out exchange.
questions.explanation: Arteries transport (thick), veins return (valves), capillaries exchange (thin).

questions.question: Describe the main disorders of the circulatory system and how they may be prevented.
questions.answer: Several disorders affect the circulatory system. HYPERTENSION is a persistent rise of blood pressure above normal (for example above 140/90 mm Hg); it strains the heart and vessels and can cause heart disease, kidney disease and stroke. ATHEROSCLEROSIS is the narrowing and hardening of arteries by the deposition of fatty material (cholesterol) and calcium, which raises pressure and reduces flow. A HEART ATTACK (myocardial infarction) occurs when a coronary artery is blocked, often by a clot on an atherosclerotic patch, so part of the heart muscle is starved of oxygen and dies; ANGINA is chest pain from insufficient blood supply to the heart muscle. These conditions can largely be prevented by a sensible low-fat diet, regular exercise, avoiding tobacco, controlling body weight and managing stress and blood pressure.
questions.explanation: Hypertension, atherosclerosis, angina, heart attack; prevention by lifestyle.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. A student observes that a cockroach and a human both have a heart, but their circulation is very different. In the cockroach the heart pumps blood into open body spaces where it bathes the organs directly, whereas in the human the blood always flows inside vessels. (a) Name the type of circulation in the cockroach. (b) Name the type of circulation in the human. (c) Give one advantage of the human type. (d) What is the insect blood called?
questions.answer: (a) The cockroach has an OPEN circulatory system, in which blood flows into open sinuses (haemocoel) and bathes the organs directly. (b) The human has a CLOSED circulatory system, in which blood always flows within a network of arteries, veins and capillaries. (c) One advantage of the closed (human) type is faster blood flow at higher pressure with better, more precise control of blood distribution to the tissues. (d) The insect blood is called HAEMOLYMPH.
questions.explanation: Open vs closed circulation, advantage, haemolymph.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. A blood test report of a patient shows a very low count of red blood cells and a low haemoglobin level. The doctor says the patient's tissues are not getting enough oxygen. (a) Name the pigment that is low. (b) State the main function of this pigment. (c) Where are RBCs produced? (d) Name the condition of low haemoglobin.
questions.answer: (a) The pigment that is low is HAEMOGLOBIN. (b) Its main function is to bind and transport oxygen from the lungs to the tissues (as oxyhaemoglobin) and to help carry carbon dioxide. (c) Red blood cells are produced in the RED BONE MARROW. (d) A condition of low haemoglobin (or low RBC count) is called ANAEMIA.
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin, oxygen transport, red bone marrow, anaemia.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. During an infection, a doctor finds that a patient's white blood cell count is much higher than normal, especially the cells that engulf bacteria. (a) What is the general function of white blood cells? (b) Name the most abundant WBC that engulfs bacteria. (c) By what process do such cells destroy bacteria? (d) Which WBCs produce antibodies?
questions.answer: (a) The general function of white blood cells is to defend the body against disease and infection. (b) The most abundant WBC that engulfs bacteria is the NEUTROPHIL. (c) Such cells destroy bacteria by the process of PHAGOCYTOSIS, in which they engulf and digest the germs. (d) The WBCs that produce antibodies are the LYMPHOCYTES.
questions.explanation: WBC defence, neutrophils, phagocytosis, lymphocytes.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. A road-accident victim of blood group A needs an urgent transfusion. The hospital has units of groups A, B, AB and O available. (a) Which antigen is present on the patient's red cells? (b) Which antibody is present in the patient's plasma? (c) Besides group A, which group could be given safely, and why? (d) What harmful reaction occurs if wrongly matched blood is given?
questions.answer: (a) The patient's red cells carry antigen A. (b) The patient's plasma contains the anti-B antibody. (c) Besides group A, group O could be given safely because O red cells have no A or B antigen and so are not attacked by the recipient's antibodies (O is the universal donor). (d) If wrongly matched blood is given, the donor red cells clump together (AGGLUTINATION), which can block blood vessels and may be fatal.
questions.explanation: Antigen A, anti-B, O donor, agglutination.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. When a person cuts a finger, bleeding soon stops as a clot forms over the wound. (a) Which blood cells begin the clotting process? (b) Which enzyme converts prothrombin into thrombin? (c) Which soluble protein is changed into insoluble fibrin? (d) Name one vitamin needed for normal clotting.
questions.answer: (a) The PLATELETS (thrombocytes) begin the clotting process by sticking to the wound and releasing thromboplastin. (b) The enzyme THROMBOPLASTIN (with calcium ions) converts prothrombin into thrombin. (c) The soluble protein FIBRINOGEN is changed into insoluble fibrin by thrombin. (d) VITAMIN K is needed for normal clotting (calcium is also required).
questions.explanation: Platelets, thromboplastin, fibrinogen->fibrin, vitamin K.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. A model of the human heart shows four chambers separated by valves, with large vessels entering and leaving it. (a) Name the upper and lower chambers. (b) Which valve lies between the left auricle and left ventricle? (c) Which vessel carries blood from the left ventricle to the body? (d) Why is the pericardium important?
questions.answer: (a) The upper chambers are the AURICLES (right and left auricle) and the lower chambers are the VENTRICLES (right and left ventricle). (b) The BICUSPID (mitral) valve lies between the left auricle and left ventricle. (c) The AORTA carries blood from the left ventricle to the whole body. (d) The pericardium is a double-walled sac containing fluid that reduces friction and protects the heart as it beats.
questions.explanation: Auricles/ventricles, bicuspid valve, aorta, pericardium role.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. Using a stethoscope, a doctor hears a repeating LUBB-DUPP sound from a patient's chest, once about every 0.8 second. (a) What do these sounds represent? (b) Which valves cause the LUBB sound? (c) Which valves cause the DUPP sound? (d) About how many times does the heart beat per minute here?
questions.answer: (a) The sounds represent the closing of the heart valves during the cardiac cycle. (b) The LUBB sound is caused by the closure of the atrioventricular (tricuspid and bicuspid) valves at the start of ventricular systole. (c) The DUPP sound is caused by the closure of the semilunar valves at the end of ventricular systole. (d) If one cycle takes about 0.8 second, the heart beats about 60 divided by 0.8, that is about 72 times per minute.
questions.explanation: Valve closures, LUBB=AV valves, DUPP=semilunar, 72 beats/min.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. A patient's heart is beating irregularly, so doctors record its electrical activity and later fit an artificial pacemaker. (a) Name the natural pacemaker of the heart. (b) Where is it located? (c) Name the record of the heart's electrical activity. (d) Name the fibres that spread the impulse into the ventricle walls.
questions.answer: (a) The natural pacemaker of the heart is the SINO-ATRIAL (SA) NODE. (b) It is located in the wall of the RIGHT AURICLE. (c) The record of the heart's electrical activity is called an ELECTROCARDIOGRAM (ECG). (d) The fibres that spread the impulse into the ventricle walls are the PURKINJE FIBRES.
questions.explanation: SA node, right auricle, ECG, Purkinje fibres.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. A nurse wraps a cuff around a patient's arm and inflates it to measure the pressure of the blood. The reading shows 120/80 mm Hg. (a) Name the instrument being used. (b) What does the figure 120 represent? (c) What does the figure 80 represent? (d) In which vessels is this pressure being measured?
questions.answer: (a) The instrument is a SPHYGMOMANOMETER. (b) The figure 120 is the SYSTOLIC pressure, the pressure in the arteries when the ventricles contract. (c) The figure 80 is the DIASTOLIC pressure, the pressure remaining when the ventricles relax between beats. (d) This pressure is measured in the ARTERIES (the force of blood against the artery walls).
questions.explanation: Sphygmomanometer, systolic 120, diastolic 80, arteries.

questions.question: Read the passage and answer the questions. A middle-aged man with a fatty diet and little exercise suddenly gets severe chest pain and is found to have a blocked coronary artery. (a) Name the condition caused by the block. (b) What fatty deposit narrows such arteries? (c) Name the milder chest pain from poor blood supply to the heart. (d) Suggest two ways to prevent such disorders.
questions.answer: (a) The condition caused by the block is a HEART ATTACK (myocardial infarction), in which the heart muscle beyond the block is starved of oxygen and part of it dies. (b) The fatty deposit that narrows the arteries is cholesterol (with calcium), causing ATHEROSCLEROSIS. (c) The milder chest pain from poor blood supply to the heart is called ANGINA. (d) Two ways to prevent such disorders are eating a sensible low-fat diet and exercising regularly (also avoiding tobacco and controlling weight).
questions.explanation: Heart attack, atherosclerosis, angina, prevention by diet and exercise.
